what_it_does: Some experimental chips use a 'spatial dataflow' design — a large fabric of many small processing elements (PEs) each running a piece of the program simultaneously, rather than one big central processor. On these chips the PEs that happen to sit physically close to the memory banks can fetch data faster than PEs far away, creating unequal access times across the fabric. Existing solutions try to move data closer to fixed PEs (a technique borrowed from multi-socket server systems called NUMA — Non-Uniform Memory Access), but that requires knowing in advance which data is 'hot,' which is often impractical. NUPEA flips the idea: instead of moving data to the PE, it moves critical load instructions to the PEs that are already physically near the memory. The compiler analyzes which data-fetch operations are on the critical path (the slowest chain of steps), and maps those fetch instructions onto near-memory PEs, while the chip exposes its own physical layout to the compiler so it can make informed placement decisions.
